genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the specialist works with athletes who swim
she starts by watching the athletes launch themselves from the edge
she looks for the movements that waste strength
she spends the second half of the day in a room full of machines
she teaches beginners to take hold of the load without tightening the upper back
she ends with a study of the session notebooks
she ran middle distances before she taught
she says her know-how comes from her own physical injuries
she rejects programs that are the same for everyone
she believes suppleness brings more progress than rigid strength
text: The strength coach at a swimming club splits her week into three clear jobs. She crouches at the pool edge first and watches her swimmers drive off the wall, following how the knees fold before the push, hunting for the small motions that burn effort and give nothing back. Afternoons belong to the weight room. There she corrects footing and teaches the youngest ones how to take hold of the bar without locking up the shoulders and the upper back. Evenings she reads the training notebooks, marking them line by line with a copyist's patience. She is short and solidly built, a former middle-distance runner, and she says her craft came from listening to her own injuries. She will not copy one athlete's program onto the next one, and she keeps repeating a single claim: a loose swimmer improves faster than a strong, stiff one.

units: the narrator tells of her visit to an indoor place devoted to climbing
her first impression of the reception was bad
the clothes lockers worked badly
she thought about giving up and leaving
an instructor taught her the right way to take hold of the grips
she lost her balance coming back down and nobody mocked her
the crowd made the place noisy later on
the way the climbers helped each other made her forget the noise
she finds the price fair and the walls well designed
she criticizes the changing rooms and means to come back
text: Right, let me say it straight: that climbing gym won me over. The front desk looked like a mess when I walked in, the lockers jammed on me, and I nearly turned around and left. Then an instructor came over and showed me how to hold the grips without crushing my fingers, and the whole session flipped. I got up an easy route, lost my footing on the way down, and nobody laughed. Later the place filled up, the noise went up a notch, and I grumbled to myself. But the climbers kept passing advice around without shoving past each other, so the racket melted into the effort. I walked out with my forearms on fire and that daft grin beginners wear once a movement finally makes sense. Fair price, smart walls, changing rooms that need gutting and rebuilding. I am going back next week, no hesitation.

units: the writer writes to a member of her family to give news
a structure that crosses a waterway was closed for works
that closure made the training circuit unusable
the person in charge moved the sessions to an old stone works
the soft ground there forces the lower joints to bend more
the pains at the back of the foot have clearly gone down
the grainy ground softens the impacts better than the hard surface
people passing saw the group from the road and signed up
the number of members has doubled
the reader is invited to come and try with borrowed equipment
text: Dear cousin, you asked how the neighborhood running club was doing. It is thriving, and the reason behind that is almost funny. The footbridge over the canal shut for repairs, which chopped our usual loop into two useless stretches. With no route left, the coach shifted our sessions out to the old stone quarry, where loose ground forces the ankles and knees to bend much more. The heel injuries fell away almost at once, because the grit soaks up the shock that concrete used to throw straight back. And since the quarry sits in plain view of the road, walkers slowed down to watch, then signed up, so we are twice the size we were. I am telling you all of this because you said you wanted to start again. Come along one morning; someone will lend you shoes, and you will find the slope loses its bite.

units: the text deals with a joint at the top of the arm left inactive
inactivity brings on a stiffening according to the fitness specialists
the discomfort felt discourages movement even further
a violent strain is not advised because it wakes the suffering again
the answer put forward consists of very small ranges repeated
the first exercise lets the limb swing freely
a very light weight such as an empty container is then brought in
if the trouble comes back one has to go back to an earlier step
the improvement does not come in a steady way
whoever rushes the process fails over and over
text: What happens to a shoulder you stop using? It seizes up, the rehab specialists answer, and the discomfort that follows discourages the movement even more. The circle closes on itself. So should you force it? No. Rough handling wakes the pain and drives the joint further into stiffness. What is left, then? A tiny range of motion, repeated without hurry, held over weeks. You begin by letting the arm hang and swing on its own, a pendulum that nothing pushes. Then you add a laughable load, an empty bottle, and after that something barely heavier. And if the ache comes back? You drop down a step without making a drama of it, since progress here almost never runs in a straight line. Whoever accepts that slowness gets a supple shoulder back. Whoever tries to skip ahead keeps staging the same disappointment over and over.

units: a specialized caregiver describes two techniques for coming back to the ground
the first technique keeps the lower limbs straight
that first option carries the shock up as far as the top of the legs
the middle joint of the leg then takes the load
the second technique bends hips and knees at the moment of contact
the muscles at the front of the leg then cushion like an elastic device
the patient finds the second option more demanding
the caregiver grants that tiredness but judges it better than wearing out the joint tissue
a noisy return to the ground points to a badly controlled cushioning
a quiet return to the ground reveals a mastered movement
text: The physical therapist was laying out for his patient two different ways of meeting the ground after a jump. The first one, he said, means coming down on straight legs: the shock then travels up with nothing in its way, right to the hips, and the knee joint has to take in almost the whole of it. The second one asks you to bend the hips and the knees the moment your feet touch, so that the muscles of the thigh brake the descent the way a spring would. The patient objected that the second method felt more tiring to him. The therapist granted him that readily, then added that tired muscle costs a great deal less than worn cartilage. He closed on a difference that beginners tend to blur: a loud landing tells you the ground took charge, while a quiet landing shows an athlete steering the whole thing himself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old physical activities are sorted into categories by the specialists
the sorting rests on the aim pursued
the first category sets two wrestlers against each other on a narrow surface
such contests are found in almost every society that settled for good
the second category gathers the speed trials over various lengths
these trials put the honor of the community at stake
the third category concerns throwing an object far away
the vocabulary of those movements survives in the disciplines of today
the fourth category brings together the ball games with local rules
these practices combined exercise ceremony and the settling of quarrels
text: Old games of movement sort themselves into distinct families, which researchers tell apart by their purpose. There are, to begin with, the trials of strength, where two opponents grapple and try to unbalance each other inside a narrow space; they turn up almost everywhere that societies settled down for good. Next come the races, run over lengths that varied widely, often barefoot, and loaded with prestige for a whole settlement. A third family gathers the throws, in which a stone, a shaft or a disc is hurled as far as the arm allows, and whose movements have handed their vocabulary down to the sports we practice now. A fourth brings together the ball games, whose rules shifted from one valley to the next. Historians add that such practices mixed exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels, with no clean line between them.

units: the contraction of a muscle obeys an ordered series of steps
the thinking organ sends an electrical impulse when an intention appears
that impulse travels along a nerve conductor
a chemical product is released at the contact zone with the fiber
very fine elements slide past each other and shorten the fiber
the attaching cord then pulls on the bony piece
the limb moves because of that pull
the filaments loosen once the movement is over
the whole process takes a very short span of time
breathing speeds up when the fibers run short of energy
text: A muscle that contracts follows a strictly ordered set of steps. It all starts in the brain, which fires an electrical signal the instant an intention to move takes shape. That signal runs down a nerve, reaches the junction where the nerve meets the fiber, and releases a chemical there. The fiber answers at once: minute filaments slide past one another and pull the whole thing shorter. The tendon, dragged by that contraction, hauls on the bone it grips, and so the limb travels. As soon as the movement ends, the filaments let go and the fiber stretches back out. The whole sequence takes a fraction of a second, and it repeats thousands of times over a single run. When it races, the runner begins to gasp, because the fibers are calling for fuel faster than breathing can bring it.

units: the narrator was coming back from a swimming session in the evening
he chose a narrow path running past a storage building
the recent rain made the slope slippery
he thought he would gain speed by going down rather than avoiding the slope
his foot skidded on a hidden root
he fell and landed in the mud
his open bag let his things spill out
he had to drag himself along the ground to gather his things one by one
a passer-by handed him back a cloth without speaking
he now takes the paved route
text: The other night, heading home from the pool, I had the bright idea of cutting along the path that runs past the warehouse. It had rained, the slope was greasy, and I told myself I would get down it faster than I would get around it. So I let my legs go, and my left foot skated off a root I never saw. I stumbled, flailed like a puppet, and landed flat in the mud with my bag hanging open. Because the bag was open, my things rolled off everywhere, and because my things rolled off everywhere, I had to crawl around gathering them one at a time. A man out for a stroll handed me my towel without a word, working very hard at not laughing. I got home soaked, caked in drying mud, and thoroughly humiliated. Now I take the paved road around, and I put a lot less pride into my shortcuts.

units: going back to running after an ankle injury worries ordinary practitioners
a badly rehabilitated joint gives way at the first badly placed step
coaches put forward an approach in four phases
the first phase consists of holding oneself up on the injured leg
that posture lasts about thirty calm breathing cycles
the second phase repeats the exercise with the eyes closed
closing the eyes removes the visual cues and calls on the receptors of the joint
the third phase brings in short hops in place with rotation of the hips
the last phase offers gentle strides with a gradual lengthening
any sharp pain calls for a stop and a return to the earlier phase
text: Going back to running after a sprain frightens most amateur athletes, and the fear is well founded: a foot joint that has not been retrained properly gives way the first time you land crooked. The routine coaches recommend comes in four stages. Start by balancing on the injured foot, arms loose along your sides, for roughly thirty calm breaths. Move on to the same position with your eyes shut, which strips the balance of every visual cue and forces the deep sensors of the foot to wake up. Then add short hops in place, turning the hips as you go and keeping the heel from drifting outward. Finish with slow strides on even ground, stretching the distance out from one session to the next. Stop everything the moment a sharp pain shows up, and pick the previous stage back up the day after.

units: two groups of runners share the same sports facility at the end of the day
the training goes on as night comes closer
the speed runners have a massive build and thick legs
they put out a violent effort over a short run of strides
they then come to a stop with their breath short
the long-distance runners are thinner and go round without a break
their breathing follows a steady rhythm
the speed specialists recover by walking
a woman in charge of the training watches both camps
she notes that one side stares at the measuring device and the other at the sky
text: The track smells of wet dust, and two groups of runners share it as the daylight goes. On one side, the sprinters: thick-set, heavy through the thighs, waiting dead still, then bursting into some thirty strides and stopping short, chests heaving, hands planted on their hips. On the other, the distance runners: leaner, looser, circling without a break, their torsos quiet, their breathing metered out like a clock. The first spend everything in one brief flare, then walk the fatigue off along the railing. The second hoard every movement and hardly ever stop. A coach watches both camps from the finish line and remarks that the sprinters keep their eyes on the timing device while the distance runners keep theirs on the sky. What they run, she says, shows in the way they carry their tiredness.
